source: YAP (Yes-associated protein) is a coactivator protein which, upon binding to TEAD proteins, stimulates their transcriptional activity.

claim: The Hippo pathway is deregulated in various cancers.
source: Since the Hippo pathway is deregulated in various cancers, designing inhibitors of the YAP:TEAD interaction is an attractive therapeutic strategy for oncology.

claim: Designing inhibitors of the YAP:TEAD interaction is an attractive therapeutic strategy for oncology.
source: Since the Hippo pathway is deregulated in various cancers, designing inhibitors of the YAP:TEAD interaction is an attractive therapeutic strategy for oncology.

claim: The Hippo signaling pathway controls organ size and tissue homeostasis in animals.

claim: The Hippo pathway is deregulated in various human cancers.

claim: Compounds that modulate Hippo pathway activity might have promise as new anticancer agents.

claim: TEAD transcription factors are the most downstream effectors of the Hippo pathway.
source: The TEAD (TEA/ATTS domain, TEAD 1–4) transcription factors are the most downstream effectors of the Hippo pathway, and several coactivator proteins interact with them, regulating their transcriptional activity (Pobbati and Hong, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Several coactivator proteins interact with TEAD transcription factors, regulating their transcriptional activity.
source: The TEAD (TEA/ATTS domain, TEAD 1–4) transcription factors are the most downstream effectors of the Hippo pathway, and several coactivator proteins interact with them, regulating their transcriptional activity (Pobbati and Hong, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The YAP protein is often overexpressed in cancers.
source: Amongst these coactivators, the YAP (Yes-associated protein) protein is often overexpressed in cancers, and targeting the YAP:TEAD interaction is emerging as a new therapeutic strategy in oncology (Gong and Yu, 2015; Felley-Bosco and Stahel, 2014; Santucci et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Targeting the YAP:TEAD interaction is emerging as a new therapeutic strategy in oncology.
source: Amongst these coactivators, the YAP (Yes-associated protein) protein is often overexpressed in cancers, and targeting the YAP:TEAD interaction is emerging as a new therapeutic strategy in oncology (Gong and Yu, 2015; Felley-Bosco and Stahel, 2014; Santucci et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The TEAD binding site of mouse YAP (mYAP) was initially mapped to the N-terminus of this protein (mYAP32-139).
source: The TEAD binding site of mouse YAP (mYAP) was initially mapped to the N-terminus of this protein (mYAP32-139) (Vassilev et al., 2001) and later on more precise knowledge was gained when the structure of the YAP:TEAD complex was published (Chen et al., 2010a; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The structure of the YAP:TEAD complex was published by Chen et al., 2010a and Li et al., 2010.
source: The TEAD binding site of mouse YAP (mYAP) was initially mapped to the N-terminus of this protein (mYAP32-139) (Vassilev et al., 2001) and later on more precise knowledge was gained when the structure of the YAP:TEAD complex was published (Chen et al., 2010a; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In crystallization studies, large protein fragments hYAP50-171 (human YAP) or mYAP35-92 were used, but electron density was only observed for the hYAP50-100 and mYAP47-85 regions.
source: In these studies, large protein fragments, hYAP50-171 (human YAP) or mYAP35-92, were used for crystallization, but electron density was only observed for the hYAP50-100 and mYAP47-85 regions.
evidence: This claim refers to data from the cited structural studies.

claim: hYAP50-171 and hYAP50-99 have a similar affinity for TEAD.
source: Subsequent binding studies showed that hYAP50-171 and hYAP50-99 have a similar affinity for TEAD (Hau et al., 2013) suggesting that the regions outside the fragment YAP50-99 have little importance for the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The regions outside the fragment YAP50-99 have little importance for the YAP:TEAD interaction.
source: Subsequent binding studies showed that hYAP50-171 and hYAP50-99 have a similar affinity for TEAD (Hau et al., 2013) suggesting that the regions outside the fragment YAP50-99 have little importance for the interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similar affinities of hYAP50-171 and hYAP50-99.

claim: Bound hYAP50-100 contains from the N- to C-terminus: a β-strand, an α-helix, a long loop and an Ω-loop.
source: Bound hYAP50-100 contains from the N- to C-terminus: a β-strand, an α-helix, a long loop and an Ω-loop.
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in the YAP:TEAD complex structure.

claim: hYAP2-268 is natively unfolded in solution.
source: The study of hYAP2-268 by nuclear magnetic resonance reveals that it is natively unfolded in solution (Tian et al., 2010) and the online ANCHOR software (Dosztányi et al., 2009) predicts hYAP50-100 to be disordered (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published NMR studies.

claim: The online ANCHOR software predicts hYAP50-100 to be disordered.
source: The study of hYAP2-268 by nuclear magnetic resonance reveals that it is natively unfolded in solution (Tian et al., 2010) and the online ANCHOR software (Dosztányi et al., 2009) predicts hYAP50-100 to be disordered (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction using ANCHOR software.

claim: hYAP50-100 becomes structured upon binding to TEAD.
source: This together with the structural data available on the bound form of YAP indicates that hYAP50-100 becomes structured upon binding to TEAD.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that YAP is disordered in solution but structured when bound to TEAD.

claim: TEAD is permanently folded and does not undergo large conformational changes upon binding to YAP.
source: In contrast, the comparison of the free and bound forms of TEAD shows that it is permanently folded and does not undergo large conformational changes upon binding to YAP (the root mean square deviation of atomic positions between TEAD in the YAP:TEAD1 complex (pdb 3KYS) and apo TEAD3 (pdb 5EMW) is 0.443 Å).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data (RMSD calculation).

claim: The root mean square deviation of atomic positions between TEAD in the YAP:TEAD1 complex (pdb 3KYS) and apo TEAD3 (pdb 5EMW) is 0.443 Å.
source: In contrast, the comparison of the free and bound forms of TEAD shows that it is permanently folded and does not undergo large conformational changes upon binding to YAP (the root mean square deviation of atomic positions between TEAD in the YAP:TEAD1 complex (pdb 3KYS) and apo TEAD3 (pdb 5EMW) is 0.443 Å).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from structural data.

claim: The contribution to binding of the β-strand from the TEAD-binding site of YAP is modest.
source: The contribution to binding of the β-strand from the TEAD-binding site of YAP is modest (Hau et al., 2013) and mainly due to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the main chain atoms of YAP and TEAD (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The β-strand contribution to binding is mainly due to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the main chain atoms of YAP and TEAD.
source: The contribution to binding of the β-strand from the TEAD-binding site of YAP is modest (Hau et al., 2013) and mainly due to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the main chain atoms of YAP and TEAD (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Only Ω-loop mimetics have a weak (around 70 µM) but measurable affinity for TEAD.
source: Studies with synthetic peptides mimicking the α-helix and the Ω-loop regions of YAP show that only Ω-loop mimetics have a weak (around 70 µM) but measurable affinity for TEAD (Hau et al., 2013; Pobbati et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published peptide studies.

claim: Mutations in the Ω-loop have a greater impact on the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex than mutations of α-helix residues.
source: Data obtained from cellular assays reveal that mutations in the Ω-loop have a greater impact on the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex than mutations of α-helix residues (Chen et al., 2010a; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published cellular assay data.

claim: Mutations of TEAD in its Ω-loop binding pocket affect the interaction with YAP to a greater extent than mutations in its α-helix binding pocket.
source: Similarly, mutations of TEAD in its Ω-loop binding pocket affect the interaction with YAP to a greater extent than mutations in its α-helix binding pocket (Chen et al., 2010a; Li et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: YAP interacts with TEAD mainly via two distinct secondary structure elements, an α-helix and an Ω-loop.
source: Overall this indicates that YAP interacts with TEAD mainly via two distinct secondary structure elements, an α-helix and an Ω-loop, and that the latter contributes most to the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on mutations and peptide mimetics.

claim: The Ω-loop contributes most to the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: Overall this indicates that YAP interacts with TEAD mainly via two distinct secondary structure elements, an α-helix and an Ω-loop, and that the latter contributes most to the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing greater impact of Ω-loop mutations.

claim: hYAP Leu65, Leu68, and Phe69 belong to the LxxLF motif.
source: In the α-helix (hYAP61-73) region, hYAP Leu65, Leu68, and Phe69 belong to the LxxLF motif, which is known to bind to hydrophobic grooves (Santucci et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by citations.

claim: The LxxLF motif is known to bind to hydrophobic grooves.
source: In the α-helix (hYAP61-73) region, hYAP Leu65, Leu68, and Phe69 belong to the LxxLF motif, which is known to bind to hydrophobic grooves (Santucci et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: hYAP Leu65, Leu68, and Phe69 are located on the same side of the α-helix making hydrophobic interactions with TEAD.
source: In the YAP:TEAD complex, these three residues are located on the same side of the α-helix making hydrophobic interactions with TEAD (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the YAP:TEAD complex structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: hYAP Met86, Leu91, and Phe95 are involved in hydrophobic interactions with TEAD.
source: In the Ω-loop region (hYAP85-99), hYAP Met86, Leu91, and Phe95 are involved in hydrophobic interactions with TEAD, and they interact with each other to form a hydrophobic core within the bound Ω-loop (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the YAP:TEAD complex structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: hYAP Met86, Leu91, and Phe95 interact with each other to form a hydrophobic core within the bound Ω-loop.
source: In the Ω-loop region (hYAP85-99), hYAP Met86, Leu91, and Phe95 are involved in hydrophobic interactions with TEAD, and they interact with each other to form a hydrophobic core within the bound Ω-loop (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the YAP:TEAD complex structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: hYAP Arg89 interacts with hTEAD4 Asp272 and Gln269.
source: hYAP Arg89 interacts with hTEAD4 Asp272 and Gln269 (Figure 1C) while hYAP Ser94 is within hydrogen bond distance from hTEAD4 Glu263 and Tyr429 (Figure 1D).

claim: hYAP Ser94 is within hydrogen bond distance from hTEAD4 Glu263 and Tyr429.
source: hYAP Arg89 interacts with hTEAD4 Asp272 and Gln269 (Figure 1C) while hYAP Ser94 is within hydrogen bond distance from hTEAD4 Glu263 and Tyr429 (Figure 1D).

claim: hYAP Phe96 does not provide any direct interaction with TEAD.
source: The amino acid hYAP Phe96 does not provide any direct interaction with TEAD.

claim: hYAP Phe96 is located above the hydrophobic core formed by hYAP Met86, Leu91 and Phe95.
source: It is located above the hydrophobic core formed by hYAP Met86, Leu91 and Phe95 (Figure 1B) and it interacts also with the guanidinium group of hYAP Arg87 (not shown, but see Zhang et al. [2014]).

claim: hYAP Phe96 interacts with the guanidinium group of hYAP Arg87.
source: It is located above the hydrophobic core formed by hYAP Met86, Leu91 and Phe95 (Figure 1B) and it interacts also with the guanidinium group of hYAP Arg87 (not shown, but see Zhang et al. [2014]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: hYAP Phe96 may contribute to the stabilization of the bound Ω-loop.
source: This residue was included in this study because it may contribute to the stabilization of the bound Ω-loop.

claim: The Kd of wt hYAP50-171 is 18 nM.
source: The Kd of wt hYAP50-171 (18 nM, Table 1) is similar to the affinity of the longer hYAP2-268 (Kd = 33 nM, [Tian et al., 2010]) showing that all the residues needed for the interaction with TEAD are probably present in hYAP50-171.

claim: The Kd of wt hYAP50-171 (18 nM) is similar to the affinity of the longer hYAP2-268 (Kd = 33 nM).
source: The Kd of wt hYAP50-171 (18 nM, Table 1) is similar to the affinity of the longer hYAP2-268 (Kd = 33 nM, [Tian et al., 2010]) showing that all the residues needed for the interaction with TEAD are probably present in hYAP50-171.

source: Each of the nine single alanine mutations of hYAP50-171 significantly destabilizes the YAP:TEAD complex (Table 1) confirming the role of the studied residues in the interaction.

claim: The hYAP Leu91Ala mutation is the most destabilizing (ΔΔG = 4.4 kcal/mol).
source: The hYAP Leu68Ala mutation is the least destabilizing (ΔΔG = ΔGmutant – ΔGwt = 1.92 kcal/mol) and the Leu91Ala mutation is the most destabilizing (ΔΔG = 4.4 kcal/mol).

source: In the α-helix region, the hYAP Phe69Ala mutation has the greatest effect on binding (ΔΔG = 3.48 kcal/mol).

claim: hYAP Phe69 is key for the interaction between the α-helix region of YAP and TEAD.
source: This residue, which is strictly conserved both in the YAP proteins and in the other TEAD coactivators TAZ and VGLL, is therefore key for the interaction between the α-helix region of YAP and TEAD.

claim: All the mutations in the Ω-loop region have a major effect on the YAP:TEAD interaction, reducing the binding energy by more than 2.5 kcal/mol.
source: All the mutations in the Ω-loop region have a major effect on the YAP:TEAD interaction, reducing the binding energy by more than 2.5 kcal/mol.

claim: Alanine mutations of hYAP Met86, Leu91, Phe95, and Phe96 may disturb stabilizing intramolecular interactions in addition to disrupting contacts with TEAD.
source: Alanine mutations of these residues may disturb these stabilizing interactions in addition to disrupting contacts with TEAD.

source: The hTEAD4 Phe373Ala (α-helix pocket) and Val414Ala (Ω-loop pocket) mutations lead to a less than twofold reduction in the affinity of hYAP50-171, showing that the contribution of these residues to the interaction is minimal (Table 2).

claim: The contribution of hTEAD4 Phe373 and Val414 to the YAP:TEAD interaction is minimal.
source: The hTEAD4 Phe373Ala (α-helix pocket) and Val414Ala (Ω-loop pocket) mutations lead to a less than twofold reduction in the affinity of hYAP50-171, showing that the contribution of these residues to the interaction is minimal (Table 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the small effect of these mutations on binding affinity.

claim: The corresponding mutations in hTEAD1 or mTEAD4 (to Phe373Ala and Val414Ala) also have a modest effect in cell-based assays.
source: The corresponding mutations in hTEAD1 or mTEAD4 also have a modest effect in cell-based assays (Li et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2010b).

claim: The hTEAD4 Glu263Ala mutation destabilizes binding with ΔΔG = 1.48 kcal/mol.
source: Within the Ω-loop binding pocket, hYAP Ser94 makes a hydrogen bond with hTEAD4 Glu263 and Tyr429 (Figure 1D) and the hTEAD4 Glu263Ala and Tyr429Phe mutations destabilize binding with ΔΔG = 1.48 and 0.81 kcal/mol, respectively (Table 2).

claim: The hTEAD4 Tyr429Phe mutation destabilizes binding with ΔΔG = 0.81 kcal/mol.
source: Within the Ω-loop binding pocket, hYAP Ser94 makes a hydrogen bond with hTEAD4 Glu263 and Tyr429 (Figure 1D) and the hTEAD4 Glu263Ala and Tyr429Phe mutations destabilize binding with ΔΔG = 1.48 and 0.81 kcal/mol, respectively (Table 2).

claim: The loss of the hydrogen bond between hYAP Ser94 and hTEAD4 Glu263 has a greater impact on binding than the loss of the hydrogen bond between hYAP Ser94 and hTEAD4 Tyr429.
source: This reveals that the loss of the hydrogen bond between hYAP Ser94 and hTEAD4 Glu263 has a greater impact on binding than the loss of the hydrogen bond between hYAP Ser94 and hTEAD4 Tyr429.

claim: The mutation corresponding to hTEAD4 Glu263Ala in hTEAD1 (Glu240) also has a significant effect on the YAP:TEAD interaction in cell-based assays.
source: The mutation corresponding to hTEAD4 Glu263Ala in hTEAD1 (Glu240) also has a significant effect on the YAP:TEAD interaction in cell-based assays (Li et al., 2010).

claim: In cells, the change to alanine/histidine in hTEAD1-2 or mTEAD4 of the tyrosine residue corresponding to hTEAD4 Tyr429 markedly reduces the interaction between YAP and TEAD.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The alanine/histidine mutations of the tyrosine corresponding to hTEAD4 Tyr429 are more destabilizing than the phenylalanine mutation studied in this work.
source: These alanine/histidine mutations are therefore more destabilizing than the phenylalanine mutation studied here.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of different mutations.

claim: The hTEAD1 Tyr421His mutation (equivalent to hTEAD4 Tyr429His) is associated with Sveinsson's chorioretinal atrophy.
source: The hTEAD1 Tyr421His mutation (equivalent to hTEAD4 Tyr429His) is also detrimental in a more physiologic context, since it is associated with Sveinsson's chorioretinal atrophy (Fossdal et al., 2004).

claim: The histidine mutation of Tyr429 probably has additional effects on the YAP:TEAD interaction beyond just preventing the formation of a hydrogen bond with hYAP Ser94.

claim: The mutation of hTEAD4 Phe337, Lys376, Leu380, and Val389 to alanine decreases ΔG by more than one kcal/mol.

claim: hTEAD4 Phe337, Lys376, Leu380, and Val389 contribute to the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: The mutation of these residues to alanine decreases ΔG by more than one kcal/mol (Table 2), showing that they contribute to the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.

claim: The mutation of the equivalent residue to hTEAD4 Val265 in hTEAD1 has a modest effect in cells on the YAP:TEAD interaction.

claim: In the YAP:TEAD complex, hTEAD4 Asp272 only interacts via its carboxylic group with the guanidinium moiety of hYAP Arg89.
source: In the YAP:TEAD complex, it only interacts via its carboxylic group with the guanidinium moiety of hYAP Arg89 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the YAP:TEAD complex structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The interaction between hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Asp272 appears to be key for the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: Since the hYAP Arg89Ala mutation also significantly reduces binding (Table 1 and [Hau et al., 2013]), the interaction between these two residues appears to be key for the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the large destabilization caused by mutations of both residues.

claim: The role of hYAP Arg89 in the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex has been demonstrated in cell-based assays.
source: The role of hYAP Arg89 in the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex has been demonstrated in cell-based assays (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: While wt TEAD4 co-immunoprecipitates with YAP, the hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutant does not to detectable levels.
source: While wt TEAD4 co-immunoprecipitates with YAP, the hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutant does not to detectable levels.
evidence: This is an experimental result from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutation prevents the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex in cells.
source: This shows that the hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutation prevents the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex in cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The transfection of wt hYAP together with wt TEAD4 in HEK293::MCAT cells stimulates the MCAT-based reporter, leading to marked luciferase activity.
source: The transfection of wt hYAP together with wt TEAD4 in HEK293::MCAT cells stimulates the MCAT-based reporter, leading to marked luciferase activity.
evidence: This is an experimental result from the luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Induction of luciferase activity is significantly reduced when hYAP is co-transfected with hTEAD4 Asp272Ala.
source: Under the same conditions, induction of luciferase activity is significantly reduced when hYAP is co-transfected with hTEAD4 Asp272Ala.
evidence: This is an experimental result from the luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutation compromises the ability of YAP to stimulate TEAD4 transcriptional activity.
source: This indicates that the mutation compromises the ability of YAP to stimulate TEAD4 transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reduced luciferase activity in the reporter assay.

claim: The hTEAD4 Asp272 mutation affects the interaction between the full-length YAP and TEAD4 proteins in a cellular context.
source: These cellular data demonstrate that the hTEAD4 Asp272 mutation affects the interaction between the full-length YAP and TEAD4 proteins in a cellular context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: The hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Asp272 interaction is key for the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex in a cellular environment.
source: Together with the published data on hYAP Arg89 (Li et al., 2010) this demonstrates that the hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Asp272 interaction is also key for the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex in a cellular environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from combining the current cellular data with published literature.

claim: Most of the ΔΔGint values for pairs of residues not located at the same binding interface are within experimental error (ΔΔGint = 0 ± 0.5 kcal/mol).
source: For the remaining pairs, most of the ΔΔGint values are within experimental error (ΔΔGint = 0 ± 0.5 kcal/mol, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: Residues in pairs with ΔΔGint = 0 ± 0.5 kcal/mol are not energetically coupled and act independently of the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: This means that the residues in these pairs are not energetically coupled and that they act independently of the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ΔΔGint values based on established principles of double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: ΔΔGint decreases with the distance between the two mutated residues with no coupling above 7 Å.
source: Earlier work on long-range effects on the additivity of mutations showed that ΔΔGint decreases with the distance between the two mutated residues with no coupling above 7 Å (Schreiber and Fersht, 1995) and that additivity is observed for distant mutations at rigid protein-protein interfaces (Wells, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Additivity is observed for distant mutations at rigid protein-protein interfaces.
source: Earlier work on long-range effects on the additivity of mutations showed that ΔΔGint decreases with the distance between the two mutated residues with no coupling above 7 Å (Schreiber and Fersht, 1995) and that additivity is observed for distant mutations at rigid protein-protein interfaces (Wells, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The residues in YAP:TEAD pairs with ΔΔGint = 0 are distant from each other by more than 9 Å.
source: Our results agree with these findings since the residues in these YAP:TEAD pairs are distant from each other by more than 9 Å and TEAD is rigid and does not change conformation upon YAP binding.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the YAP:TEAD complex structure.

claim: Significant coupling (ΔΔGint = −0.62 kcal/mol) was observed between hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Lys376.
source: We also measured ΔΔGint < −0.5 kcal/mol for one pair with residues belonging to each binding interface – hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Lys376 (−0.62 kcal/mol).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Lys376 appear to act in a synergistic manner on the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: While they are located in two distant pockets at the YAP:TEAD interface, these two residues appear to act in a synergistic manner (ΔΔGint < 0) on the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative ΔΔGint value.

claim: An electrostatic component may explain the ΔΔGint value measured between hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Lys376.
source: Since electrostatic interactions have a long-distance effect, an electrostatic component may explain the ΔΔGint value measured between these amino acids.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed coupling energy.

claim: Within the α-helix, 5 ΔΔGint values below −0.5 kcal/mol were measured for residues located in close proximity.
source: Within the α-helix, 5 ΔΔGint values below −0.5 kcal/mol were measured for residues located in close proximity: hYAP Leu65:hTEAD4 Lys376 (−0.65 kcal/mol), hYAP Leu68:hTEAD4 Phe337 (−0.65 kcal/mol), hYAP Phe69:hTEAD4 Lys376 (−1.28 kcal/mol), Leu380 (−1.01 kcal/mol) and Val389 (−1.11 kcal/mol) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative results from the double mutant cycle analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The low to moderate ΔΔGint values in the α-helix may reflect the van der Waals nature of the interactions between these residues.
source: These low to moderate ΔΔGint values may reflect the van der Waals nature of the interactions between these residues, since such interactions usually give lower coupling energies (Schreiber and Fersht, 1995; Goldman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: hYAP Phe69 is significantly coupled (ΔΔGint < −0.95 kcal/mol) to the 4 TEAD residues studied.
source: hYAP Phe69 is significantly coupled (ΔΔGint < −0.95 kcal/mol) to the 4 TEAD residues studied (Table 2), highlighting once more the importance of this residue at the α-helix binding interface.
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative results from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: Significant ΔΔGint values were measured between residues that are not directly in contact: hYAP Leu65:hTEAD4 Val389 (−0.52 kcal/mol) and hYAP Phe69:hTEAD4 Phe337 (−0.95 kcal/mol).
source: Significant ΔΔGint values were also measured between residues that are not directly in contact: hYAP Leu65:hTEAD4 Val389 (−0.52 kcal/mol) and hYAP Phe69:hTEAD4 Phe337 (−0.95 kcal/mol).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: hYAP Phe69 and hTEAD4 Phe337 may act synergistically in holding/orienting the hYAP α-helix in its correct bound orientation.
source: hYAP Phe69 and hTEAD4 Phe337, which are located at each side of the bound α-helix (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), may act synergistically in holding/orienting the hYAP α-helix in its correct bound orientation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the high coupling energy between these residues, supported by structural data.

claim: In the Ω-loop interface, 12 ΔΔGint values below −0.5 kcal/mol were measured.
source: In the Ω-loop interface, 12 ΔΔGint values below −0.5 kcal/mol were measured (Table 3, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative results from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: Significant coupling (−0.96 kcal/mol) was observed between hYAP Ser94 and hTEAD4 Glu263.
source: Significant coupling (−0.96 kcal/mol) was observed between hYAP Ser94 and hTEAD4 Glu263, two residues within hydrogen bond distance (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: hYAP Arg89, Leu91, and Phe95 are coupled to hTEAD4 Glu263, albeit to a lesser extent than hYAP Ser94.
source: hYAP Arg89, Leu91, and Phe95 are also coupled to hTEAD4 Glu263, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative results from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: Coupling between hYAP Arg89, Leu91, Phe95 and hTEAD4 Glu263 might be indirect and mediated via hYAP Ser94.
source: Since these 3 YAP residues are not in contact with hTEAD4 Glu263, coupling might be indirect and mediated via hYAP Ser94.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the coupling energies.

claim: Secondary coupling via a third side chain was previously described in other systems.
source: Secondary coupling via a third side chain was previously described in other systems (Schreiber and Fersht, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The largest coupling energy was observed between hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Asp272, ΔΔGint = −3.49 kcal/mol.
source: The largest coupling energy was observed between hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Asp272, ΔΔGint = −3.49 kcal/mol (Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: Once hYAP Arg89 is mutated, the hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutation has little effect on binding (ΔΔG4 = 0.04 kcal/mol).
source: The double mutant cycle shows that, once hYAP Arg89 is mutated, the hTEAD4 Asp272Ala mutation has little effect on binding (ΔΔG4 = 0.04 kcal/mol, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the double mutant cycle analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The larger effect on binding of the hYAP Arg89Ala mutation against an hTEAD4 Asp272Ala background (ΔΔG2 = 0.85 kcal/mol) can be explained by the loss of both additional intermolecular interactions with TEAD and intramolecular stabilizing interactions in the bound YAP.
source: The larger effect on binding of the hYAP Arg89Ala mutation against an hTEAD4 Asp272Ala background (ΔΔG2 = 0.85 kcal/mol, Figure 4A) can be explained by the loss of both additional intermolecular interactions with TEAD (Figure 1C) and intramolecular stabilizing interactions in the bound YAP (Hau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the double mutant cycle data supported by structural observations and citations.

claim: hTEAD4 Asp272 is strongly coupled (ΔΔGint < −1.6 kcal/mol) to each of the hYAP Ω-loop residues studied.
source: hTEAD4 Asp272 is also strongly coupled (ΔΔGint < −1.6 kcal/mol, Table 3) to each of the hYAP Ω-loop residues studied.
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative results from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: No significant coupling energy was measured between hTEAD4 Asp272 and hYAP Leu68 (ΔΔGint = −0.02 kcal/mol).
source: This effect is limited to these amino acids, since no significant coupling energy was measured between hTEAD4 Asp272 and hYAP Leu68, which is located in the α-helix region (ΔΔGint = −0.02 kcal/mol, Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the double mutant cycle analysis.

claim: Hydrophobic/polar Ω-loop residues are indirectly coupled to hTEAD4 Asp272 via hYAP Arg89.
source: These hydrophobic/polar Ω-loop residues are therefore indirectly coupled to hTEAD4 Asp272 via hYAP Arg89, because they make no direct contact with this amino acid.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the coupling energies and structural data.

claim: The hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Asp272 interaction is crucial for the binding of the Ω-loop, since it allows several residues to act in a synergistic manner on the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: The hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Asp272 interaction is thus crucial for the binding of the Ω-loop, since it allows several residues to act in a synergistic manner on the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double mutant cycle analysis showing strong coupling between Asp272 and multiple Ω-loop residues.

claim: Several proline residues – hYAP Pro85, Pro92, Pro98, and Pro99 – are present in the Ω-loop, where they play a role in complex formation.
source: Several proline residues – hYAP Pro85, Pro92, Pro98, and Pro99 – are also present in the Ω-loop, where they play a role in complex formation (Hau et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Proline residues in the Ω-loop are difficult to study with the techniques used in this report, because their mutation may affect the local structure of YAP in addition to disrupting interactions with TEAD.
source: However, these residues are difficult to study with the techniques used in this report, because their mutation may affect the local structure of YAP in addition to disrupting interactions with TEAD.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the limitations of the mutagenesis approach.

claim: hYAP Phe69 is a 'hot-spot' residue at the α-helix interface.
source: We show that hYAP Phe69 is a 'hot-spot' residue at the α-helix interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the large destabilization caused by the Phe69Ala mutation and its coupling to multiple TEAD residues.

claim: hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Lys376 act in a synergistic manner in the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
source: We find that hYAP Arg89 and hTEAD4 Lys376, which are not located at the same binding interface, act in a synergistic manner in the formation of the YAP:TEAD complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative coupling energy measured between these residues.

claim: The hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Asp272 interaction is essential for the interaction between the Ω-loop region of YAP and TEAD.
source: We reveal that the hYAP Arg89:hTEAD4 Asp272 interaction is essential for the interaction between the Ω-loop region of YAP and TEAD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the large coupling energy and the effects of mutations on this interaction.

claim: Evidence is provided for the key role of hTEAD4 Asp272 in the interaction between YAP and TEAD both in vitro and in a cellular context.
source: We provide evidence for the key role of hTEAD4 Asp272 in the interaction between YAP and TEAD both in vitro and in a cellular context.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from both in vitro binding assays and cellular assays.

claim: The purified hTEAD4 protein is 100% acylated at hTEAD4 Cys367.
source: The purified hTEAD4 protein is 100% acylated at hTEAD4 Cys367.
evidence: This is a characterization of the protein preparation used in the study.
